                                         techniques for fictional characters (e.g. see [9, 11, 23]) and their integration into a story (e.g. Campbell’s Monomyth
                                         template [4]).

TL-E003.exact_quote:
In Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), conversation
                                         is a user interface paradigm (e.g. chatbots), recently also successfully employed to interact with text [38].

TL-E004.exact_quote:
The etymology of character points to a stamping tool – figuratively, a person’s
stamp of personality [10]. Our Progressive Manifestation concept picks up on this with the idea of painting a “blank”
chatbot into a character by adding information.

TL-E005.exact_quote:
Therefore, we build on the model of Forster [15] who distinguishes
characters as “flat” (based on a single quality) or “round” (more than one factor). Related considerations of complexity
appear in more extensive later models (e.g. Hochman [21], Fishelov [14]). While both types can be useful, we focus
on round characters because they present the harder challenge: Forster [15] emphasises achieving roundness by
considering multiple qualities, which motivates our Guided Conversation Mode.

TL-E006.exact_quote:
Practically, for the construction of fictional characters we consider writing guides and frameworks (e.g. Egri [11], McKee
[26], Seger [30]), which all support writers with conceptual categories: Concretely, we build on the attributes from the
character “bone structure” by Egri [11], which covers the three categories physiology (e.g. age, eye and hair colour),
psychology (e.g. values, ambitions, skills), and sociology (e.g. social background, education, community), enriched with
attributes elicited in our survey (see Section 2.2.2).

TL-E007.exact_quote:
A related character model by Rimmon-Kenan [29]2 articulates complexity, development, and penetration into inner
life.

TL-E008.exact_quote:
asking the character-bot about goals and opinions (cf. a character’s “dramatic goal” and “position” by Field
[13]) might also stimulate plot ideas by the writer.

TL-E009.exact_quote:
Finally, both modes together can be compared to a distinction made
by McKee [26] about “characterization” (observable attributes – included in our guided prompts) vs “true character”
(below the surface, including decisions – e.g. asking the bot about decisions and actions in the open chat).

TL-E010.exact_quote:
CharacterChat is a concept and tool in the tradition of creativity support
tools (CSTs) [31, 32]. Based on the definition by Frich et al. [16], CSTs are “employed to positively influence users of
varying expertise in one or more distinct phases of the creative process”.

TL-E011.exact_quote:
Writing tools in the (HCI) literature support academic writing [36], stories [8, 39], poetry [19], metaphors [18],
and slogans [8], using NLP [8, 18, 19, 36], visualisations [39] or images [5]: For instance, Storyprint plots scenes and
characters on a “circular time axis” [39].

TL-E012.exact_quote:
NLP researchers explored (controlled) story plot generation with AI [37],
including (reinforcement learning) agents [1, 25, 28], which (inter)act as characters to create the plot.

TL-E013.exact_quote:
Others used agents as a proxy audience during story creation [27]. Further work focused on author characteristics:
InkWell [17] uses computational optimisation to generate text variants based on data-driven author personas.

TL-E015.exact_quote:
In short, we found great diversity in writing approaches, in line with related work [23].
As a key takeaway, writers overall cover a wide range of aspects when describing their characters, yet not everyone
thinks about everything.

TL-E016.exact_quote:
The list of 31 attributes is based on the survey and literature [11] and could be flexibly
extended in the future.

TL-E017.exact_quote:
In addition, we integrate ConceptNet [35]6 as a knowledge base to suggest
attribute values (e.g. the “physical examination” and “zombie” in Fig. 2a).

TL-E018.exact_quote:
For the Open Conversation Mode, we used a publicly available
Deep Learning language model released by HuggingFace [40], described as “a conversational AI with a persona”7: It
generates text based on both the chat history and a few sentences about the chatbot’s “personality”.

TL-E020.exact_quote:
Finally, people filled in the
Creativity Support Index (CSI) questionnaire [6].

TL-E024.exact_quote:
Note that the CSI questionnaire here asks questions about
collaboration with “other people” [6], which was not a function in this prototype. The very low factor score indicates
that people also did not find this aspect to be relevant here.

TL-E029.exact_quote:
We reflect on our concept through the lens of the framework for studying co-creative AI by Guzdial and Riedl [20]:
Therein, user and AI take turns to work on an “artifact” with two actions: First, artifact actions shape a created artifact
(here: character).

TL-E030.exact_quote: Overall, we thus realise a co-creative [20] and mixed-initiative [22] concept: User and AI take turns to shape the outcome.

TL-E033.exact_quote:
First,
recent discussions in HCI distinguish between AI as a tool and as emulation [33]. Here, we illustrate a new combination:
CharacterChat is a creative tool for writers and an emulation of the resulting character.

TL-E001.exact_quote:
Large language models (LLMs) can be applied to a wide range of
problems, ranging from creative writing assistance [8, 26, 36, 44] to
code synthesis [13, 14, 20].

TL-E002.exact_quote:
Users currently customize these models
to specific tasks through strategies such as prompt engineering [4],
parameter-efficient tuning [19], and fine-tuning [10].

TL-E003.exact_quote:
More
specifically, some users want to be able to critique the model’s
outputs to specify how they should be different [5]. We call this
customization strategy interactive critique.

TL-E004.exact_quote:
When interacting with a chatbot like ChatGPT1 [28] or Bard2,
interactive critique will often alter the chatbot’s subsequent re-
sponses to conform to the critique.

TL-E005.exact_quote:
In the context of model customization, Constitutional AI [1]
offers a specific customization strategy involving natural language
principles.

TL-E006.exact_quote:
Earlier chatbots employed rule-based approaches to construct a
dialogue flow [11, 29, 42], where the user’s input would be matched
to a pre-canned response written by the chatbot designer.

TL-E007.exact_quote:
Later on,
supervised machine learning approaches [43, 48] became popular,
where chatbot designers constructed datasets consisting of ideal
conversational flows.

TL-E008.exact_quote:
Large, pre-trained models like
Chat-GPT [28] can hold sophisticated conversations out of the box,
and these models are already being used to create custom chatbots
in a number of domains, including medicine [18].

TL-E009.exact_quote:
Recent work has shown that users would also like to steer
LLMs by interactively critiquing its outputs; during the conversation
they refine the model’s outputs by providing follow-up instructions
and feedback [5].

TL-E010.exact_quote:
A new approach to steering LLM-based chatbots (and LLMs
in general), called Constitutional AI [1] involves writing natural
language principles to direct the model.

TL-E012.exact_quote:
To help users find a better phrasing for their prompt, automatic
approaches have been developed that search the LLM’s training
data for a more effective phrasing [27, 32].

TL-E001.exact_quote:
Preregistration is the practice of documenting a study’s objective
and analysis plan prior to conducting it and observing its out-
comes [62].

TL-E002.exact_quote:
To do so, public preregistration repositories, such as the Open Sci-
ence Framework (OSF) [29] and AsPredicted [48], are available
across disciplines.

TL-E003.exact_quote:
boosts the credibility of quantitative [61], qualitative [34, 49], and
exploratory research [21].

TL-E004.exact_quote:
A growing number of research commu-
nities advocate preregistration, including in medicine for clinical
trials [18, 37], psychology [61], economics [66], biology [31], politi-
cal science [59], and human-computer interaction [14].

TL-E005.exact_quote:
While efforts encouraging preregistration are also underway in
the HCI community [15, 43, 44, 70], adoption is still in its early
stages [14, 15].

TL-E008.exact_quote:
Given that the vast majority of CHI publications report
on at least one study [52], we conclude that preregistration in the
HCI research community remains a rare practice.

TL-E009.exact_quote:
In the learning sciences, scaffolding refers to supporting learners
with concrete structure and guidance to ensure successful com-
pletion of a task [77, 93].

TL-E010.exact_quote:
The term has been adopted in the HCI
community to refer to step-by-step instructions, such as providing
non-experts with a structured workflow required for designing
rigorous scientific experiments [68].

TL-E011.exact_quote:
Current preregistration platforms, including domain-specific and
domain-general registries, support researchers in various disci-
plines [61]. Domain-specific registries exist for clinical trials [64],
economics [6], and political science [36].

TL-E012.exact_quote:
Furthermore, over 1,100
journals and conferences have implemented the Transparency and
Openness Promotion (TOP) guideline, a standard addressing open
science practices, which include study and analysis preregistra-
tion [61].

TL-E013.exact_quote:
In contrast to domain-specific registries, AsPredicted [65]
offers a domain-general preregistration template, where researchers
answer nine questions about their research designs and analyses.

TL-E014.exact_quote:
The Open Science Foundation (OSF) [28] offers
another domain-general registry, where authors preregister in fields
such as social and behavioral science, education, business, and life
science.

TL-E015.exact_quote:
Researchers can also use open registra-
tion by posting a customized PDF instead of the form on existing
registries [62].

TL-E016.exact_quote:
Preregistration can help research teams to reach consensus on spe-
cific research procedures at an early stage in their work [83].

TL-E017.exact_quote:
signing a research study typically demands that researchers identify
abstract concepts, determine measures, assign different conditions,
formulate hypotheses, and decide sample sizes, among other study-
specific requirements [40, 90].

TL-E018.exact_quote:
As a result, it encourages collaboration and team science
that facilitates complete and high-powered study designs [60].
Preregistration also promotes trustworthy and transparent anal-
ysis.

TL-E019.exact_quote:
Researchers have argued that it may mitigate HARKing (Hy-
pothesizing After Results are Known [46]), a sloppy research prac-
tice of post hoc “fishing” for a significant effect after data has been
collected [81].

TL-E020.exact_quote:
In response,
preregistration timestamps any variables, hypotheses, and analy-
sis plans before data collection, mitigating “questionable research
practices” [39].

TL-E021.exact_quote:
Evidence in clinical trials shows that preregistra-
tion reduced the number of studies that rejected null hypotheses
from 57% to 8% [42].

TL-E022.exact_quote:
As a result, it de-emphasizes a commonly
used dichotomous threshold (e.g., p < 0.05) and reinforces rigor-
ous study designs and method planning [94].

TL-E023.exact_quote:
Researchers may be
                                                                          more likely to conduct risky but rigorously planned studies that
                                                                          could produce null results [15].

TL-E024.exact_quote:
this weakens the “file-drawer effect” [73], whereby stud-
ies that do not reach the critical threshold are more likely to be
rejected for publication and kept hidden.

TL-E025.exact_quote:
A recent study of 27 papers with preregistered
badges in Psychological Science found that all published studies
deviated from the preregistered plans, but only one explained the
deviation [13].

TL-E026.exact_quote:
Yamada [94] noted that researchers could selectively
report data by over-issuing multiple preregistrations or “preregister-
ing” after completing an experiment.

TL-E027.exact_quote:
Instead of solely emphasizing
preregistration, some researchers argue that a reputable scientific
report should focus on whether an analysis is appropriate given
the nature of the data [50, 63, 69, 76].

TL-E028.exact_quote:
Compared to quanti-
tative methods, qualitative studies emphasize the qualities of a
particular technology and how people interact with it, thus gener-
ating theories or hypotheses rather than testing hypotheses based
on experimental manipulation [4, 80].

TL-E029.exact_quote:
For example, qualitative re-
searchers may apply thematic or grounded theory analysis for data
collected from ethnographic, interview, focus groups, diary or ob-
servational studies [4].

TL-E030.exact_quote:
The high level of subjectivity in qualitative
studies might challenge the notion of preregistration, which gen-
erally promotes replication of objective findings [78].

TL-E031.exact_quote:
call for preregistration and even transparency in research, primar-
ily focusing on quantitative methods, has provoked disagreement
among qualitative scholars in other social-science fields [15, 38, 49].

TL-E032.exact_quote:
For example, the Qualitative Transparency Deliberations (QTD), a
three-year deliberative process by hundred of political scientists,
questioned the usefulness of research transparency [38].

TL-E033.exact_quote:
In summary, preregistration does not address all questionable
research practices [39, 94] and adapting preregistration to qualita-
tive studies is open for discussion in the broader research commu-
nity [15, 38, 49].
